# Introduction 

For developers, the Trackyverse uses [Air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/) 
as a default formatter/linter to quickly reformat code. This article providers 
instructions on why we use Air and how to setup Air whether you are using 
RStudio, VS Code, or Positron. 

Air shares properties with other modern formatters and linters, such as Ruff for Python.

A few things to note about Air: 

- Air is highly opinionated and offers relatively few options for customization but it can be customized. 
- Air is written in Rust and is based on the Biome formatter engine, which makes it extremely fast.

# Formatting 

**Why does formatting matter? and why does using a linter matter?**

Formatting code creates consistency in the style of the code written. 
It does not change the meaning of code, but instead allows for easier 
readablity and reporduciblity. Consistency, readability, and reproducibility
are highly important for coding projects in general but become 
of even greater importance when projects have multiple developers. 

Using a common linter matters because it enforces adhering to a given style.
An agreed-upon set of rules are applied to all files of a particular type e.g., `.R`. 
A linter applies these rules every time a file is saved which  streamlines the overall 
use of a given style.  

For example, a prescribed style could recommend including whitespace after arguments 
(e.g., `c(1, 2, 3)` versus `c(1,2,3)`), enforce newlines after function closures, and all 
manner of rules and standards. Rules about code indenting with the appropriate amount of 
leading whitespace depending on the context. For more information about formatting and style 
details of Air see [Air formating details](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/formatter.html) 

To understand the linting rules that are enforced by Air see [How does Air format my code?](https://tidyverse.org/blog/2025/02/air/#how-does-air-decide-how-to-format-your-code)

# Installation
Trackyverse packages recommend using Air as a linter and formatter to enforce the standard style 
across all changes you make to your code / files.

To install Air at the command line, you can use one of the following commands.

On macOS and Linux:

`curl -LsSf https://github.com/posit-dev/air/releases/latest/download/air-installer.sh | sh`

On Windows:

`powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://github.com/posit-dev/air/releases/latest/download/air-installer.ps1 | iex"`

This will automatically add Air to your PATH. The very first time you install Air, after 
adding it to your PATH variable with the command above, you’ll need to restart your terminal.

For a specific version of Air:

`curl -LsSf https://github.com/posit-dev/air/releases/download/0.9.0/air-installer.sh | sh`

`powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://github.com/posit-dev/air/releases/download/0.9.0/air-installer.ps1 | iex"`

If you’re on macOS and are familiar with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/), which we highly recommend, you can 
alternatively install the [Air formula](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/air) with:

`brew install air`

If you use [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), you can install Air via the [air-formatter](air-formatter) package:

```bash 
# Global install
uv tool install air-formatter
air format path/to/my/script.R
```

```bash
# Invoke once without installing
uvx --from air-formatter air format path/to/my/script.R
```

Note that if you’d like to use Air inside of IDEs like VS Code or Positron, install the Extension for those editors, 
which comes pre-bundled with an Air binary, so there’s nothing you need to do besides [download the Extension](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/editor-vscode.html).

# Setup

## RStudio

If you are using RStudio, it does not support [Language Server Protocol](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/), but you can still use Air as an *external* formatter. 

To get Air working with RStudio see the following guide - [using Air with RStudio](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/editor-rstudio.html), 
which details how to adjust RStudio's Global Options to find and recognize Air. See [Guide to using Air](#guide-to-using-air) below.

## Positron and VS Code 

If you are using Positron or VS Code, it does support Language Server Protcols and allows for Air to have a bit more freedom, enforcing 
different settings at a user level and at a workspace level (i.e. for just the current project you are working on). 

Because Air can leverage Language Server Protcols there is no further setup needed.

# Initialization 

To setup Air for a repository, once installed, you can run the following code: 

```r
install.packages("usethis")
```

We can then use `{usethis}` to setup Air for a repository:

```r
usethis::use_air()
```

This will create a `air.toml` file and a folder `.vscode` wherein it will create two config files: `settings.json` and `extensions.json`.

The `settings.json` file contains the following: 

```json
{
    "recommendations": [
        "Posit.air-vscode"
    ]
}
```

The `extensions.json` file contains the following this: 

```json
{
    "[r]": {
        "editor.formatOnSave": true,
        "editor.defaultFormatter": "Posit.air-vscode"
    },
    "[quarto]": {
        "editor.formatOnSave": true,
        "editor.defaultFormatter": "quarto.quarto"
    }
}
```

Both `settings.json` and `extension.json` can be further customized such as: 

```json
{
    "[r]": {
        "editor.formatOnSave": true,
        "editor.defaultFormatter": "Posit.air-vscode"
    }
}
```

# Guide to using Air

Once we have setup Air on a repository we can do a couple different things to start using it with our code 

## RStudio

To enable features such as Format on Save we can adjust the Global Settings using `Tools -> Global Options -> Code -> Saving and check Reformat documents on save.`, which is detailed in [Air's guide to using with RStudio](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/editor-rstudio.html#rstudio-format-on-save). 

## Positron and VS Code 
To enable features like Format on Save, you’ll need to adjust settings in either your user or workspace level `settings.json` file. We generally recommend modifying workspace level settings for two reasons:

- Workspace level settings exist inside your workspace folder at `.vscode/settings.json` and are checked in to your version control system. This means that your collaborators will get those settings automatically when they check out your project. User level settings are not checked in to version control.

- User level settings are automatically applied for all projects that you open. While this sounds nice, if you open an older project (or a project you don’t own) that doesn’t use Air, then you’ll have to remember to turn off your user level Air settings before committing to that project, otherwise you may create a large amount of format related diffs that the project may not want.

The easiest way to set up a workspace level `settings.json` with the recommended settings is by running the command *Air: Initialize Workspace Folder*. This is equivalent to running `usethis::use_air()` from an R console.

Alternatively, to open your `settings.json` file from the Command Palette (`Cmd + Shift + P` on Mac/Linux, `Ctrl + Shift + P` on Windows):

Run Preferences: `Open Workspace Settings (JSON)` to modify workspace specific settings (recommended).
Run Preferences: `Open User Settings (JSON)` to modify global user settings.

At this point, for the Trackyverse, there is no futher setup needed, however, for more on using Air to its 
full capacity, see the [Air Guide](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/editor-vscode.html). 

# Customizing Air

The `air.toml` file is a Tom's Own Markup Language (toml) file that allows users to customize and change the default 
settings of Air. 

Below are the available settings to adjust and customize and can be added to to `air.toml` file: 

```toml
[format]
line-width = 80
indent-width = 2
indent-style = "space"
line-ending = "auto"
persistent-line-breaks = true
assignment-style = "arrow"
exclude = []
default-exclude = true
skip = []
table = []
default-table = true
```
